coffee-decaffeinated-pre-lightened-and-p.title: Decaffeinated Coffee, Pre‑lightened and Pre‑sweetened with Low‑Calorie Sweetener

content.title: About
content.content: Decaffeinated coffee, pre‑lightened and pre‑sweetened with a low‑calorie sweetener (5216) is a ready‑to‑drink product from which natural caffeine has been removed, then lightly roasted and blended with a low‑calorie sweetener. It retains the aromatic notes of traditional coffee while lacking the stimulating effect.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Decaffeination is usually performed with water or CO₂, preserving most flavor compounds.
Pre‑lightening reduces bitterness and yields a milder taste, favored by fans of light roasts.
Low‑calorie sweeteners (e.g., stevia or erythritol) do not raise blood sugar and add virtually no calories.
Decaf coffee is often enjoyed in the evening to avoid sleep disturbances.
Pre‑sweetening allows immediate consumption without adding sugar.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Even without caffeine, the drink retains polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Coffee stimulates gastric secretions, which can aid digestion even in its decaf form.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: The low‑calorie sweetener provides a sweet taste without significantly increasing energy intake.

items.title: May reduce blood pressure spikes
items.content: Absence of caffeine lowers the risk of temporary blood pressure elevation in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Hydration support
items.content: Decaf coffee contributes to daily fluid intake without the stimulating effect of caffeine.

items.title: Coffee allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to coffee components.

items.title: Residues from decaffeination
items.content: Some decaffeination methods may leave trace solvents; choose products with proper certification.

items.title: Sweetener tolerance
items.content: Certain individuals may experience gastrointestinal discomfort from erythritol or other polyol sweeteners.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Even without caffeine, coffee remains acidic and can irritate the stomach lining if consumed in excess.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Dissolve 1–2 teaspoons of the product in hot water (80–90 °C) and stir. Optionally add milk, plant‑based alternatives, or spices such as cinnamon or vanilla. Suitable as a hot or cold beverage.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in a tightly sealed container protected from light. For extended shelf life, keep refrigerated to preserve aroma.

content.title: About
content.content: Raw garlic is the edible bulb of the plant Allium sativum, widely used in cooking and traditional medicine. It has a sharp, pungent flavor and a distinctive aroma that develops when its cells are broken.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Garlic belongs to the onion family and is closely related to onions, leeks, and shallots.
There are more than 600 garlic varieties, differing in size, skin color, and flavor intensity.
Garlic was used in ancient Egypt, Greece, and Rome as food, medicine, and a protective agent against parasites.
When dried, the cloves become garlic powder, which retains most of the active compounds.
Garlic can repel certain insects, so it is sometimes used as a natural repellent.

items.title: Rich in allicin
items.content: When garlic is crushed or chopped, allicin forms – a compound with antioxidant and anti‑inflammatory properties.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Studies suggest regular garlic consumption may help lower blood pressure and cholesterol levels.

items.title: Boosts immunity
items.content: Sulfur compounds and B‑vitamins in garlic help enhance the body’s resistance to infections.

items.title: Antioxidant
items.content: Vitamin C and selenium aid in neutralizing free radicals, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Prebiotic fibers in garlic promote the growth of beneficial gut bacteria.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to garlic, ranging from skin rashes to gastrointestinal symptoms.

items.title: Gastrointestinal irritation
items.content: Large amounts of raw garlic can cause heartburn, gas, or irritation of the stomach lining.

items.title: Interaction with medications
items.content: Garlic may enhance the effects of anticoagulant drugs, so moderation is advised for people on blood thinners.

items.title: Body odor
items.content: Sulfur compounds released during metabolism can lead to a characteristic garlic breath and body odor.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw garlic can be minced, thinly sliced, or made into a paste. Add it to sauces, marinades, salads, and vegetable dishes in small amounts to preserve its flavor and benefits.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store garlic heads in a cool, dry, well‑ventilated place away from direct light. If needed, keep them in the refrigerator in a paper bag, but avoid airtight containers to prevent mold growth.

content.title: About
content.content: Rice milk is a plant‑based beverage made from whole rice, water, and sometimes added ingredients such as salt, sugar, or flavorings. It has a light yellow color, a gentle sweet taste, and a thin texture. It is commonly used as a dairy‑milk alternative for people with lactose intolerance, dairy‑protein allergy, or vegan diets.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Rice milk first appeared in Japan in the early 20th century as an inexpensive milk substitute.
Unlike soy milk, rice milk is naturally free of common allergens like soy and nuts.
It contains less protein than cow’s milk but is rich in carbohydrates, especially starch.
Manufacturers often add vegetable oils (e.g., sunflower or rapeseed) to improve flavor and mouthfeel.
Rice milk generally has a longer shelf life after opening compared with most other plant milks.

items.title: Low allergen content
items.content: Suitable for people allergic to dairy proteins, soy, nuts, and gluten.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Provides thiamine (B1), niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Contains modest amounts of iron that contribute to blood formation.

items.title: Digestive friendly
items.content: Lactose‑free, making it gentle for those with lactose intolerance.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Has less saturated fat than whole cow’s milk, which may help manage cholesterol levels.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: The high amount of simple carbs can cause a rapid rise in blood sugar.

items.title: Low protein content
items.content: Not a primary protein source, especially for athletes and children.

items.title: Added sugars
items.content: Some commercial versions contain added sugar, increasing calorie count.

items.title: Arsenic presence
items.content: Rice can contain trace amounts of heavy metals; choose reputable brands.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drink rice milk on its own, add it to cereals, smoothies, coffee, baking, and sauces. For a creamier texture, blend with a little vegetable oil or coconut milk.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the opened container in the refrigerator and consume within 5‑7 days. Avoid exposure to direct sunlight. Discard if the milk develops off‑smell, discoloration, or off‑taste.

content.title: About
content.content: Sweet potato (batata) is a root vegetable rich in vitamins and minerals. Baked without added fat (NS) retains its natural flavor and aroma, offering a soft, slightly sweet flesh and a crisp skin.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sweet potatoes contain more beta‑carotene than regular potatoes, giving them a bright orange color.
Baking enhances aromatic compounds, making the taste more intense.
Batata originated in Central and South America but is now cultivated worldwide.
Sweet potatoes can be used in desserts, soups, and even as chips.
They provide complex carbohydrates that promote lasting satiety.

items.title: Rich in beta‑carotene
items.content: Beta‑carotene converts to vitamin A, supporting vision, immunity, and skin health.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C boosts antioxidant protection and aids iron absorption.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber improves digestion and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium maintains electrolyte balance and normal blood pressure.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Baked without added fat makes it suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to sweet potato.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Sweet potatoes contain oxalates, which can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible people.

items.title: Overconsumption
items.content: Large portions may raise blood sugar due to the high carbohydrate content.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Baked sweet potato can be enjoyed as a standalone side, added to salads, soups, toast, or used as a base for mash. Feel free to sprinkle spices such as cinnamon, paprika, or rosemary for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store baked sweet potato in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat in the oven or microwave to restore a crisp skin.
